title: Geometric proof (two-column)
examples: How do I start a two-column proof?
What kind of reasons can I use in a proof?
Does the 'given' part go in the proof?

explain.say: Today we learn to write geometric proofs using two columns. This method keeps your statements and reasons very clear.
First, you must clearly state what is given and what you need to prove. These are your starting points for the proof.

draw.text: Given: Information known. Prove: What needs proving.

explain.say: The first statement in your proof is always the 'given' information. The reason is that it is stated as true.
Next, you use theorems or definitions to write subsequent statements. The reason column explains why your statement is true.
For example, if two lines are parallel, then alternate interior angles are equal. This is a key theorem to use.

draw.text: If line a || line b, then angles are equal.

faq.q: What should I write in the 'given' section of my proof?
faq.a: You write down all the facts that the question tells you are true. These are the starting assumptions for your proof.
asks: Where do I list what I know?

faq.q: Is the 'prove' statement the last thing I write?
faq.a: No, the 'prove' statement is what you aim to reach. It is the final statement you must logically deduce.
asks: What is the goal of the proof?
How do I know when I am finished?

faq.q: Can I use my own ideas as reasons in a proof?
faq.a: No, your reasons must come from established geometric theorems or definitions. You cannot just assume something is true.
asks: Can I just say it's true?
What counts as a valid reason?

faq.q: If I use a theorem, do I need to name it?
faq.a: Yes, it is best practice to name the theorem or postulate you are using. This shows your reasoning is sound.
asks: Should I write down the theorem name?
How do I cite my source?

faq.q: What if the question gives me too much information?
faq.a: If you are given extra information, you can use it to help prove the main point. Just make sure every step connects logically.
asks: Can I use all the given parts?

facts: A two-column proof has two main parts: statements and reasons.
The 'given' section lists the initial facts accepted as true.
The 'prove' statement is the conclusion you must reach.
Reasons must be based on definitions, postulates, or theorems.

quiz.say: If two angles are complementary, what is the relationship between them?

options.show: One angle is double the other.
options.say: One angle is double the other.

quiz.why: Complementary angles, by definition, must add up to exactly 90 degrees.

wrong.0: This describes a specific ratio, not the general rule for complementary angles.
wrong.1: Equal angles are only required if the angles are both 45 degrees.
wrong.3: This is the definition for supplementary angles, which is a different concept.

quiz.say: In a two-column proof, where does the 'given' information belong?

options.show: In the statements column, listed first.
options.say: In the statements column, listed first.

options.show: At the end of the proof.
options.say: At the end of the proof.

quiz.why: The 'given' facts are your starting assumptions, so they are listed as the first statements.

wrong.1: The 'given' facts are statements of fact, so they belong in the statements column.
wrong.2: The proof must start with what is known to build towards the conclusion.
wrong.3: The structure requires the two-column format for clarity and rigor.

quiz.say: If you know two sides of a triangle are equal, what can you conclude about the angles opposite them?
quiz.show: Angles opposite equal sides are equal.

options.show: The sum of the angles is 180 degrees.
options.say: The sum of the angles is 180 degrees.

options.show: The angles opposite them are equal.
options.say: The angles opposite them are equal.

options.show: The angles must be right angles.
options.say: The angles must be right angles.

quiz.why: This is the Isosceles Triangle Theorem, which states that equal sides mean equal opposite angles.

wrong.0: While true for all triangles, this does not use the information about the equal sides.
wrong.1: The triangle only needs two sides to be equal, not all three.
wrong.3: This is only true for a specific type of right-angled triangle.
